title: How Spam Filters Learn
objective: After this level you can explain how a spam filter learns from labeled examples which words and signals predict junk mail.
summary: Graham's 2002 filter counted words in a spam pile and a good-mail pile; labeled examples teach it, and every Report spam click keeps it learning as spam evolves.

cards.headline: One of the best spam clues Paul Graham ever found was "ff0000".
cards.body: It's the web code for bright red. In 2002 his filter found it about as telling as any rude word. He never told the filter to look for red. It found that clue on its own, from examples.

cards.headline: Two piles and a lot of counting
cards.body: Graham's essay "A Plan for Spam" laid out the method. Start with one pile of known spam and one pile of good mail. Count how often every word appears in each pile. A word common in spam but rare in good mail gets a high spam probability; your best friend's name gets a low one. A new email is scored by combining the probabilities of its most telling words.

cards.headline: The labels do the teaching
cards.body: Each email in those piles comes labeled: spam or not spam. The filter works out which features predict the label. Machine learning people call this supervised learning, training on labeled examples, and spotting spam is one of its standard examples. The piles are the teacher.

cards.headline: Your clicks keep it learning
cards.body: Graham argued everyone should have two delete buttons: ordinary delete and delete-as-spam, so each person's piles keep growing from their own mail. Gmail's Report spam button feeds the same kind of learning: Google says that as you report more spam, Gmail identifies similar emails as spam more efficiently. That matters because spam keeps changing, and a filter that learns from new examples changes with it.

cards.headline: Filter: trained
learned: Graham's filter counted words in a spam pile and a good pile
Counts become the probability that an email is spam
Labeled examples teach it: supervised learning
Report spam clicks keep it learning as spam evolves

questions.prompt: What did Graham's filter count to learn what spam looks like?

options.label: The number of recipients on each email
How often each word appears in spam and in good mail
How long each email took to arrive
options.rationale: Delivery time isn't what it counted.

options.label: How many links each sender had ever posted
options.rationale: It counted words in two piles of mail.

questions.explanation: It counted each word in a pile of spam and a pile of good mail, then turned the counts into spam probabilities.

questions.prompt: Why does a spam filter need to keep learning from new reports?

options.label: Spam keeps changing, and the filter must change with it
Old reports expire after a week
options.rationale: Nothing says reports expire; spam evolves.

options.label: The filter forgets words when the power goes off
Each email can only be checked once
options.rationale: The point is new kinds of spam keep appearing.

questions.explanation: Spam evolves, so a filter that keeps learning from newly reported mail keeps up with new tricks.

questions.prompt: Before a filter can count words, the letters must be stored somehow. Per Level 4, what is each character inside the computer?

options.label: A tiny drawing of the letter's shape
options.rationale: The device draws the shape; the character itself is a number.

options.label: A sound sample of the letter
A pixel on the screen
options.rationale: Pixels show text; they don't store it.

options.label: A unique number from a code such as Unicode

questions.explanation: Unicode gives every character a unique number, so words are stored as numbers a filter can count and compare.
